{{Short description|Partial differential equation}}
The '''Cole–Hopf transformation''' is a change of variables that allows to transform a special kind of [[Parabolic partial differential equation|parabolic]] [[partial differential equation]]s (PDEs) with a quadratic nonlinearity into a [[Heat equation|linear heat equation]]. In particular, it provides an explicit formula for fairly general solutions of the PDE in terms of the initial datum and the [[heat kernel]].

Consider the following PDE:

<math display="block">u_{t} - a\Delta u + b\|\nabla u\|^{2} = 0, \quad u(0,x) = g(x)</math>

where <math>x\in \mathbb{R}^{n}</math>, <math>a,b</math> are constants, <math>\Delta</math> is the [[Laplace operator]], <math>\nabla</math> is the [[gradient]], and <math>\|\cdot\|</math> is the [[Euclidean norm]] in <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>. By assuming that <math>w = \phi(u)</math>, where <math>\phi(\cdot)</math> is an unknown [[Smoothness|smooth function]], we may calculate:

<math display="block">w_{t} = \phi'(u)u_{t}, \quad \Delta w = \phi'(u)\Delta u + \phi''(u)\|\nabla u\|^{2}
</math>

Which implies that:

<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
w_{t} = \phi'(u)u_{t} &= \phi'(u)\left( a\Delta u - b\|\nabla u\|^{2}\right) \\
&= a\Delta w - (a\phi'' + b\phi')\|\nabla u\|^{2} \\
&= a\Delta w
\end{aligned}
</math>

if we constrain <math>\phi</math> to satisfy <math>a\phi'' + b\phi' = 0</math>. Then we may transform the original nonlinear PDE into the canonical [[heat equation]] by using the transformation:

{{Equation box 1|cellpadding|border|indent=:|equation=<math> w(u) = e^{-bu/a} </math>|border colour=#0073CF|background colour=#F5FFFA}}This is ''the'' ''Cole-Hopf transformation''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Evans |first=Lawrence C. | authorlink=Lawrence C. Evans|title=Partial Differential Equations |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=2010 |isbn= |edition=2nd |series=Graduate Studies in Mathematics |volume=19 |pages=206–207}}</ref> With the transformation, the following initial-value problem can now be solved:

<math display="block">w_{t} - a\Delta w = 0, \quad w(0,x) = e^{-bg(x)/a}
</math>

The unique, bounded solution of this system is:

<math display="block">w(t,x) = {1\over{(4\pi at)^{n/2}}} \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} e^{-\|x-y\|^{2}/4at - bg(y)/a}dy</math>

Since the Cole–Hopf transformation implies that <math>u = -(a/b)\log w</math>, the solution of the original nonlinear PDE is:

<math display="block">u(t,x) = -{a\over{b}}\log \left[ {1\over{(4\pi at)^{n/2}}} \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} e^{-\|x-y\|^{2}/4at - bg(y)/a}dy \right]
</math>

The complex form of the Cole–Hopf transformation can be used to transform the [[Schrödinger equation]] to the [[Madelung equations|Madelung equation]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Madelung |first=E. |date=1927 |title=Quantentheorie in hydrodynamischer Form |journal=Die Naturwissenschaften |language=de |volume=40 |issue=3–4 |pages=322–326 |doi=10.1007/BF01504657 |issn=1434-6001}}</ref>

== Applications ==

* [[Aerodynamics]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cole |first=Julian D. |authorlink=Julian Cole |date=1951 |title=On a quasi-linear parabolic equation occurring in aerodynamics |url=https://www.ams.org/qam/1951-09-03/S0033-569X-1951-42889-X/ |journal=Quarterly of Applied Mathematics |language=en |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=225–236 |doi=10.1090/qam/42889 |issn=0033-569X|doi-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* Stochastic [[optimal control]]
* Solving the [[Burgers' equation#Viscous Burgers' equation|viscous Burgers' equation]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hopf |first=Eberhard | authorlink=Eberhard Hopf | date=1950 |title=The partial differential equation u<sub>t</sub> + uu<sub>x</sub> = μ<sub>xx</sub> |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cpa.3160030302 |journal=Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics |language=en |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=201–230 |doi=10.1002/cpa.3160030302|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* [[Madelung equations|Madelung equation]]
